usecases.title: Run a Hermes agent
usecases.seoTitle: Hermes agent hosting: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I want a personal assistant that answers me on Telegram, remembers what I tell it and runs jobs on a schedule.
usecases.standfirst: Hermes is a personal AI agent you host yourself. It needs a small machine that stays on and keeps its files. Two providers offer it in one click (Agent 37 with no terminal at all, DigitalOcean as a Marketplace server image); most can run it if you can follow terminal instructions; a few are a poor fit for an assistant that never sleeps.
whatItIs: [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent) is an open-source (MIT) assistant from Nous Research. You talk to it from Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, email and [20+ other apps](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/), it keeps a memory of you between conversations, and it writes itself reusable skills from what it does.

The model (Claude, GPT, an open model) runs elsewhere and is billed by its own provider. What you host is the small program that holds your memory, your logins and your schedule, and that runs commands, browses and edits files for you. That program is what this page is about.

Its own README says to run it "on a $5 VPS, a GPU cluster, or serverless infrastructure that costs nearly nothing when idle". A sandbox provider is one of those choices: the difference is how easy it is to set up, whether it is allowed to stay on, and what it costs when it is waiting.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: At least 1 CPU and 1 GB of memory; 2 CPUs and 2 to 4 GB recommended, and at least 2 GB if it uses the browser. 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB leaves room for Chromium and a growing memory.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes, usually. By default it fetches Telegram messages by asking Telegram every few seconds, and the docs say plainly that "a polling bot can never sleep". It also runs your scheduled jobs every 60 seconds. Webhook mode lets it sleep on hosts that wake on an incoming request, but scheduled jobs then do not fire while it sleeps.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Everything in ~/.hermes: memory, past conversations, skills, scheduled jobs, API keys and chat logins. A provider that deletes the disk when the machine stops loses all of it.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: A browser is optional and is the hungriest part. Docker is optional. A GPU is only needed if you run the model yourself.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting. Battleships' always-on assistant workload averages about 6% CPU, with peaks near 100% when it browses or runs a command. That is why providers that charge only for CPU actually used come out cheap here.

twoWays.title: Two ways to use a sandbox with Hermes
body: **Host Hermes on the machine.** Hermes itself lives in the sandbox: it holds your memory, answers your messages and runs around the clock. This is what most people mean, and it needs a provider that lets a machine stay on and keeps its disk.

**Keep Hermes where it is, send its commands to a sandbox.** Hermes runs on your laptop or server, and only the shell commands it decides to run go to a cloud sandbox, so a mistake cannot damage your own machine. Hermes has this built in for [Modal, Daytona and Vercel Sandbox](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/configuration), and Fly.io publishes the same for [Sprites](https://docs.fly.io/sprites/integrations/agent-plugins.md). It is cheap, because the sandbox only runs while a command does, but it is not hosting: your own machine still has to be on.

routes.what: Pick Hermes on the Personal plans and it is set up with a dashboard, task board, web terminal and chat channels. The free plan sleeps when idle; paid plans stay up between scheduled jobs.
routes.price: Personal plans from $3.99 a month; $29.99 with a built-in browser

routes.what: Hermes is already installed on every sandbox. Create one with auto-stop turned off, run the setup wizard over SSH, and keep the gateway running as a service.
boxd documents the personal-assistant pattern: create a machine, install the assistant, turn off auto-hibernate (otherwise it sleeps after four quiet hours) and let chat apps reach it.
Nothing preinstalled and no guide. Create a sandbox with auto-stop off, run Hermes' installer over SSH, and keep the gateway running as a service.
Start a sandbox from the dashboard and you get a shell in the browser; install Hermes there and mark the sandbox persistent so it never idle-pauses. No Hermes guide.
The dashboard creates a machine and opens a browser terminal and desktop; installing Hermes and keeping it running is typed by hand. No Hermes template.
The dashboard creates a sandbox and opens a terminal; Hermes is installed by hand. Lizard's one-click templates cover OpenClaw, not Hermes.
Create a Devbox, install Hermes over SSH, and turn on wake-on-HTTP so it pauses between messages and wakes when one arrives.

E2B ships a ready-made hermes template you start from its command line. Sessions end after 24 hours on Pro and one hour on the free plan, so it suits Hermes doing tasks better than an assistant that never stops.

A built-in Hermes backend: Hermes on your own machine starts, stops and resumes a Daytona sandbox for its commands. Daytona's dashboard Playground opens a browser terminal if you want to host it there instead.
A built-in Hermes backend for running its commands. Not an always-on host: Modal sandboxes end after 24 hours and cannot pause.
Vercel publishes an official guide, but it is for the backend mode: Hermes stays on your computer and each task runs in a sandbox.

Fly.io markets Sprites for agents like Hermes, but its only official Hermes integration is the backend mode. Hosting Hermes inside a Sprite means registering it as a service, because a Sprite pauses about 30 seconds after activity stops.
Possible in a sandbox with a volume for its files, installed by hand. Blaxel's agent hosting caps a run at 15 minutes, so it is not the place for an always-on assistant.
Neither Cloudflare nor Hermes documents this. Cloudflare sandboxes also lose their disk when they stop, so memory would have to be saved elsewhere.

Create a named sandbox with `--timeout 0` on Pro, install Hermes and keep it in a background process or under systemd. Suspend is the catch: Hermes polls Telegram every few seconds, so the sandbox has to stay running, and only Pro allows a session with no cap. Everything in `~/.hermes` sits on the ephemeral root disk, so a snapshot or a mounted volume is what saves it if the sandbox is ever terminated.

The Marketplace 'Hermes Agent' image creates a Droplet with Hermes, Node and the OpenAI SDK installed. The listing publishes no post-deploy steps beyond the API example, so expect to add a model key and a channel in the console.

picks.for: If you do not want a terminal
picks.why: The only provider here that sets up Hermes in one click with no terminal at all. Plans run from $3.99 a month (1 vCPU / 4 GB / 8 GB, bring your own model key) to $29.99 (2 vCPU / 8 GB / 20 GB, with a built-in browser).
picks.watch: The free plan sleeps after 15 idle minutes. These Personal plans are a separate product from the Agent 37 Cloud machines the calculator prices.

picks.for: If you can follow terminal steps
picks.why: Hermes is preinstalled on a full virtual machine. The small size running all month is $13.14 of usage, inside the $20 monthly plan.
picks.watch: Auto-stop is on by default, so create the machine with it turned off. A stopped machine's disk is kept for only 14 days, and there is no free plan.

picks.for: If you want to pay least for waiting
picks.why: It charges for CPU only while it works, so an assistant that mostly waits costs about $25 a month at 2 vCPU / 4 GiB, and a persistent sandbox never idle-pauses.
picks.watch: No Hermes guide, one US region, and storage keeps billing while the machine is stopped.

usecases.outside: Hermes' own docs point to an ordinary virtual private server ("a $5 VPS") or Docker on a machine you own. Neither isolates the agent the way a sandbox does, and neither is set up for you.

usecases.title: Run an OpenClaw agent
usecases.seoTitle: OpenClaw hosting: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I want OpenClaw answering me on WhatsApp or Slack, with its own browser and memory, without keeping my laptop on.
usecases.standfirst: OpenClaw is a self-hosted assistant built around one always-on gateway. It has more official hosting guides than Hermes: three providers deploy it in one click, and four more publish a guide or template.
whatItIs: [OpenClaw](https://docs.openclaw.ai/help/faq/what-is-openclaw) is an open-source assistant you run on your own infrastructure, for yourself or a team. It replies on the apps you already use, including WhatsApp, Slack, Telegram, Discord, Signal and iMessage, and can read files, run commands, browse and keep memory.

Its centre is the **Gateway**, which the docs call "the always-on control plane": one long-running program that holds every chat connection and hands messages to the agent. Hosting OpenClaw means hosting the Gateway.

Models run through their own APIs, so no GPU is needed. A team can share one Gateway, but the docs are clear that one Gateway is one trust domain: people who do not trust each other need separate ones.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: At least 1 core, 1 GB of memory and 500 MB of disk; 2 GB or more recommended. OpenClaw's Fly.io guide uses 2 shared CPUs and 2 GB. 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB gives the browser room.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes. The Gateway owns the chat connections, and Telegram uses outbound polling by default. Webhook mode needs a public HTTPS address that is always reachable.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: ~/.openclaw (config, a SQLite database and chat logins) and the agent's workspace (memory and personality files). Lose the WhatsApp credentials and you scan the QR code again.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: A browser is optional; OpenClaw can drive its own Chrome profile. Docker is optional and tool sandboxing is off by default. No GPU for API models.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting: about 6% CPU on average in Battleships' always-on assistant workload, which names OpenClaw, with peaks near 100%.

routes.what: OpenClaw is one of the six agents on the Personal plans, set up in one click and driven from the browser.
routes.price: Personal plans from $3.99 a month; $29.99 with a built-in browser

routes.what: A Deploy OpenClaw template on Lizard's app platform builds the Gateway, creates its access token and gives it a public HTTPS address.
OpenClaw publishes a Daytona guide, and OpenClaw is preinstalled in Daytona's default image. Create the sandbox with auto-stop off, connect over SSH and run onboarding.
An official, experimental template: one always-on container with its database copied to R2 storage. OpenClaw estimates roughly $40 to $50 a month. Setup is by command line with Wrangler.
A ready-made openclaw template and a gateway guide. Sessions end after 24 hours on Pro, so staying on needs your own restart logic.
A Vercel walkthrough installs OpenClaw in a sandbox and links WhatsApp by QR code. Sessions end after 24 hours on Pro.
An official tutorial, which says the install is manual: a sandbox, a volume for its files, and onboarding in the terminal.
The OpenClaw command is preinstalled but the Gateway does not start by itself. Turn auto-stop off and run the Gateway as a service.
boxd's personal-assistant page is written around OpenClaw: install it, turn off bot protection so chat apps can reach it, and turn off auto-hibernate.
Install OpenClaw in a sandbox with auto-stop off and run the Gateway as a service. No guide.
A browser shell from the dashboard, then a manual install in a persistent sandbox. No guide.
The dashboard creates a machine with a browser terminal and desktop; the install is typed by hand.
Install it in a Sprite and register the Gateway as a service so it comes back after the Sprite pauses. No guide.
Install it in a Devbox over SSH and expose its port. No guide.
Not documented by either side, and Modal sandboxes end after 24 hours.

SSH into a named sandbox on Pro, install OpenClaw and run the Gateway there, with the sandbox kept awake by the Gateway's own traffic. Tensorlake publishes no OpenClaw guide. Crabbox, the CLI from OpenClaw, does have a Tensorlake provider, but it syncs a repo and runs a test suite — it does not host the Gateway, so it is not a route to an OpenClaw agent.

link.title: Tensorlake: a sandbox as your dev environment

routes.what: The hardened OpenClaw image provisions a Droplet with Caddy and a Let's Encrypt certificate, a generated gateway token, device pairing, container isolation, fail2ban and unattended upgrades. You still copy the gateway token and pair a device.

picks.for: If you do not want a terminal
picks.why: One-click OpenClaw on the same Personal plans as Hermes, from $3.99 a month, with a built-in browser from the $29.99 plan.
picks.watch: The free plan sleeps after 15 idle minutes, and these plans are separate from the Cloud machines the calculator prices.

picks.for: If you want one click and a public address
picks.why: The Deploy OpenClaw template gives the Gateway an HTTPS address and a token from the browser, inside a $19 monthly plan that comes back as usage.
picks.watch: The template runs on Lizard's app platform, billed at $0.025 per vCPU-hour and $0.0125 per GB-hour, not at the sandbox sizes the calculator uses.

picks.for: If you want OpenClaw's own guide
picks.why: OpenClaw documents Daytona itself, and the default image already has it installed. $200 of free compute covers the first month or so.
picks.watch: Each sandbox's disk is capped at 10 GiB, and a 2 vCPU / 4 GiB machine on all month is about $122.

picks.for: A cheap, hardened, always-on OpenClaw with its own public address
picks.why: A $12/month Droplet arrives with TLS, a gateway token, device pairing, container isolation and fail2ban already configured, on a real VM with root and 16 regions.
picks.watch: Powering off does not stop the bill, and the $12 tier is the floor only since the February 2026 update; the January image needed $24.

usecases.outside: OpenClaw also documents ordinary hosts. Hostinger sells a one-click managed OpenClaw from $4.99 a month on a two-year term, renewing at $11.99. OpenClaw's Fly.io guide estimates $10 to $15 a month. Railway and Northflank have one-click templates with no price on the guide. Render's free tier sleeps after 15 minutes, which breaks an always-on Gateway.

usecases.title: Give a coding agent its own machine
usecases.seoTitle: Cloud machines for Claude Code and Codex, compared
usecases.question: I want Claude Code or Codex to work on my code in the cloud, not on my laptop.
usecases.standfirst: A coding agent reads a repository, edits files and runs tests. In a sandbox, a mistake cannot touch your laptop, and the work carries on when the laptop is closed. Several providers ship Claude Code and Codex already installed.
whatItIs: Tools like [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup) and Codex run in a terminal: you give them a task, they read the code, change it and run commands to check their work. Running them in a cloud sandbox gives each one a disposable Linux machine with your repository on it.
Unlike a personal assistant, a coding agent does not need to stay on. It runs while you work and can stop at night, as long as the repository, its caches and the agent's login survive.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Claude Code needs 4 GB of memory or more. Anthropic's own cloud sessions allow up to about 4 vCPU, 16 GB and 30 GB of disk. 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 40 GiB covers the agent, tests and a few containers.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. It runs during working hours; eight hours on 20 days is 160 hours a month.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The repository and uncommitted work, the agent's login (~/.claude for Claude Code), and caches and Docker images if you want a fast start.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: Docker helps when tests need databases or services. A browser matters only for checking web interfaces. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting on the model: about 4% CPU on average in Battleships' software-factory workload, with short peaks during builds.

routes.what: Seven coding agents on every sandbox, including Claude Code and Codex; boat prompt runs one for you.
Every machine ships with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.
Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and others are installed on every machine.
Claude Code and Codex come installed, with a desktop you can open in the browser.
Choose the claude or codex template when creating a sandbox.
Claude Code and Codex are on the one-click Personal plans, on your own Anthropic or OpenAI account.
routes.price: Personal plans from $3.99 a month; $29.99 with a built-in browser

routes.what: An official guide for running Claude Code, Codex and Amp in E2B sandboxes from code.
An official guide for running Claude Code in a sandbox from the Daytona command line.
An official guide: Claude Code edits a GitHub repository in a sandbox and returns a diff.
Each Claude Code session gets its own sandbox, through Vercel's agent harness.

The first-party route is the `tensorlake-opencode` plugin: OpenCode keeps running on your laptop and its bash, read, write, edit and patch calls run in a sandbox that survives restarts and can mount a volume or a hosted Git repository. Claude Code and Codex are not in the images, but they work over SSH or VS Code Remote-SSH, and Tensorlake has self-hosted guides for Claude Managed Agents, Cursor Cloud Agents and Devin Outposts.
Install Claude Code or Codex on a Droplet yourself; the default images have no coding agent. A 2 vCPU / 4 GiB Basic Droplet at $24/month is enough for one developer.
routes.price: $24 a month for 2 vCPU / 4 GiB, on or powered off

picks.for: One machine per developer
picks.why: Claude Code and Codex preinstalled on a full VM with Docker. The 4 vCPU / 8 GB size for 160 hours is about $6 of usage, inside the $20 plan.
picks.watch: Auto-stop is on by default, which suits this job, and a stopped disk is kept for 14 days.

picks.for: If you want memory billed on use
picks.why: Three coding agents preinstalled, memory billed on what is actually in use, and a 100 GiB disk billed only for what is written.
picks.watch: CPU is billed on the full size while running, and the 4 vCPU size comes with 16 GiB.

picks.for: One fresh sandbox per task, from code
picks.why: Built for starting sandboxes from your own program, with an official coding-agent guide and pausing that keeps memory and files at no charge.
picks.watch: Disk is 10 GiB on the free plan and 20 GiB on Pro, and sessions longer than an hour need the $150 Pro plan.

usecases.outside: Anthropic runs Claude Code cloud sessions on its own machines for Claude subscribers, and OpenAI runs Codex Cloud for ChatGPT plans. Neither publishes a separate machine price on its docs page.

usecases.title: Run code inside your own product
usecases.seoTitle: Code interpreter sandboxes for your product, compared
usecases.question: My app lets users or an LLM run code, and I need somewhere safe to run it.
usecases.standfirst: A code interpreter is a sandbox your application calls: send code, get back the output, the errors and any files. Each run is short and thrown away, so the price of a second of compute, how quickly a sandbox starts and how many can run at once matter more than anything else.
whatItIs: This is infrastructure you build into a product, not something your users log into. Your server asks the provider's API for a sandbox, runs the code, collects the result and throws the sandbox away.

The code is untrusted by definition, so isolation is the first question: whether each run gets its own kernel, and what it can reach on the network. The [isolation](/features/isolation/) and [outbound network](/features/outbound-network/) pages compare that.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Small. Provider minimums run from 0.125 of a core and 128 MiB on Modal upwards. Battleships' interpreter workload uses 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 5 GiB and fills 80% of that memory, so 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 10 GiB is the safer size.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. Each run lasts seconds to minutes; 20,000 one-minute runs a month is about 650 a day.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Usually nothing. Results go back to your app or your own storage.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: About 17% CPU on average in Battleships' interpreter workload. Charging by the second, and only for CPU actually used, both matter here.

routes.what: Its original use: a code-interpreter SDK and per-second billing.
Sandboxes started from an SDK, billed per second, with $200 of free compute.
Sandboxes from Python or JavaScript, sized down to a fraction of a core.
Firecracker sandboxes from an SDK, with CPU billed only while working.
Sandboxes started from a Worker, with CPU billed only while working.

Wrap `sandbox.run()` as a `run_code` tool and keep one sandbox per session so installed packages and written files carry between calls; the Tool Calls page has Claude, OpenAI and OpenAI Agents SDK examples. Pre-install the usual libraries in a snapshot so each session starts warm, and turn egress off or to an allowlist before running model-written code.

Harness Runtime runs each session in a Firecracker microVM through doctl, PyDo or the API. Medium (2 vCPU / 4 GB) is $0.126 an hour at full allocation, with CPU and memory billed separately from storage.

picks.for: The default choice
picks.why: Built for exactly this. At the workload below it is about $55 a month at list price, and the free plan's one-time $100 credit covers most of the first two months.
picks.watch: The free plan limits sessions to an hour and disk to 10 GiB. Concurrency limits are per plan.

picks.for: If runs mostly wait
picks.why: CPU is billed only while working, so the same workload is about $13 a month.
picks.watch: Smaller company, one US region, and a free tier capped at four sandboxes at once.

picks.for: If your app already runs on Cloudflare
picks.why: Started from a Worker next to your code, with CPU billed only while working.
picks.watch: The smallest size that has 2 vCPU also has 8 GiB of memory, which you pay for. There is a $5 monthly account minimum.

usecases.outside: Anthropic's hosted code-execution tool runs Claude's code for you with no sandbox to manage: 1 CPU, 5 GiB, no internet, 1,550 hours included and then $0.05 per container-hour.

usecases.title: Run a browser or computer-use agent
usecases.seoTitle: Hosting a browser or computer use agent, compared
usecases.question: I want an agent that opens websites, clicks and fills in forms, or uses a whole desktop.
usecases.standfirst: Browser agents drive a real Chromium, or a whole desktop with a mouse and keyboard. Memory is the constraint, not CPU, and logins are the thing people forget to keep.
whatItIs: A browser agent reads pages as text or screenshots and clicks, types and scrolls like a person. A computer-use agent does the same with a full desktop. Both need a machine with a display and enough memory for Chromium.
Sessions are usually short and thrown away. If the agent must stay logged in to sites, keep its browser profile, which means keeping the disk or saving a snapshot.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 10 GiB for a browser; Browserless gives the same minimum. A full desktop is more comfortable at 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 20 GiB.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. Typical sessions are minutes long.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Nothing, unless logins must survive: then the browser profile and cookies.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: About 3% CPU on average; Chromium's memory is what fills the machine.

routes.what: Boot `tensorlake/ubuntu-vnc`, which ships XFCE, TigerVNC, Firefox and Chrome, then either drive the desktop through `connectDesktop()` for screenshots, clicks and typing, or start Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` and tunnel it to localhost so Playwright, Puppeteer or `chrome-devtools-mcp` drive it as if it were local. Snapshot a warmed profile so parallel agents start with cookies already in place.
Harness Runtime sessions include chromium and a browser-automation tool, but there is no desktop and no live preview of a running app.

picks.for: A desktop you can watch
picks.why: The agent-browser image comes with a desktop and Chromium you can open from the dashboard, and an idle machine pauses itself and wakes when its preview link is used.
picks.watch: The free plan is one 4 vCPU / 8 GiB machine that pauses after 30 idle minutes.

picks.for: Full VMs at a flat rate
picks.why: A full Ubuntu VM with room for a browser, at a flat hourly price per size.
picks.watch: At thousands of sessions a month, the plan's start limits apply, and paid starts come out of the wallet.

picks.for: Computer use from code
picks.why: Documents computer use, with sandboxes started from an SDK and per-second billing.
picks.watch: Each sandbox's disk is capped at 10 GiB.

usecases.outside: Browser services such as Browser Use Cloud sell hosted browser time (from $0.02 per browser-hour) without a machine to manage.

sources.label: Battleships: browser and computer-use workloads (built by the Boat team)

usecases.title: Host your own n8n
usecases.seoTitle: n8n hosting: where to self-host n8n and what it costs
usecases.question: I want n8n running my automations around the clock, on a server I control, without paying per workflow run.
usecases.standfirst: n8n is a visual automation tool you can host yourself. It needs a small machine that never sleeps and keeps its database. Two providers set it up in one click; most others can run it if someone follows terminal steps; the task-only sandboxes are the wrong place for it.
whatItIs: [n8n](https://docs.n8n.io/) is a workflow automation tool. You draw a workflow on a canvas: a **trigger** (something that starts it, such as a form being sent or a time of day), then steps that call other apps, reshape data or ask an AI model. Its [README](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n) counts 1,500+ ready-made connections.

Hosting it yourself means you run the server, its database, its encryption key and its upgrades. In return there is no per-run fee: n8n's own hosted [n8n Cloud](https://n8n.io/pricing/) is billed by how many workflow runs you use.

Most workflows start in one of two ways: a **webhook**, which is a web address another app calls when something happens, or the [Schedule Trigger](https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/core-nodes/n8n-nodes-base.scheduletrigger), n8n's own built-in clock. Both only work while n8n is running, which decides what kind of machine it needs.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: n8n publishes no self-hosting minimum. Its Cloud plans run from 640 MiB of memory to 4 GiB, and the software alone uses about 180 MiB. Because any single step can pull a large file into memory, 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB is the safer buy.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes. n8n listens for webhooks only while it runs, and the Schedule Trigger works "in a similar way to the Cron software utility": its clock lives inside the machine. A sleeping machine misses both. A host that wakes on a web request can still catch webhooks after a short delay, but scheduled runs will not fire while it sleeps.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The database (workflows, saved logins to other apps, run history; SQLite by default, PostgreSQL for anything larger) and the encryption key n8n creates on first start. Without that key the saved logins cannot be read, and a database backup alone will not bring them back.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: No browser on the server: the editor opens in yours. The documented install uses Docker (a standard way to package and run software); npm on Node.js 20.19 to 24.x is the alternative. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting. No benchmark measures n8n; Battleships' nearest always-on workload averages about 6% CPU, with peaks near 100% when a large workflow runs. Size for the peak, not the average.

routes.what: A Deploy Now template creates an n8n app and a separate managed PostgreSQL database, connects them and gives n8n a public HTTPS address. It does not set an encryption key, attach a volume or add worker processes.

The agent37-n8n template runs the official n8n image with a public editor address and SQLite on a disk that is kept. The dashboard asks only for an owner password, and auto-sleep is off by default; leave it off for scheduled workflows.
routes.price: Default 2 vCPU / 4 GB instance at $4.76 a month

routes.what: A full Ubuntu machine with Docker. Install n8n as a service that comes back after a restart, make its port public, and keep the disk. No n8n guide, and no custom domains.
Docker is preinstalled and running, and custom domains are self-serve. Turn hibernation off so schedules fire. No n8n template or guide.

Create a sandbox with auto-stop turned off (it stops after 15 idle minutes by default), install n8n with npm and make its port public. n8n names Daytona as the sandbox for its own AI Assistant feature, which is not the same as hosting n8n there.
The agent-browser image includes Docker. Turn auto-pause off, install n8n and publish port 5678. No n8n guide.
A Devbox can serve n8n and wake when a request arrives, but a paused Devbox's clock stops, so scheduled workflows need it kept running. No n8n guide.
Docker, persistent sandboxes ("no idle pause") and custom domains are all documented, which is what n8n needs. No n8n guide.
Create a sandbox with auto-stop and idle pause off, install n8n, run it as a service and make its port public. No n8n guide.
Blaxel's n8n page is about n8n calling a Blaxel agent, not about hosting n8n. Running n8n itself would be a manual install with a volume for its database.
Command line only, and a Sprite pauses when idle unless something holds it awake. Its fixed large size is far more than n8n uses. No guide.
A poor fit: "stopping the instance deletes the files on its disk", so n8n's database and encryption key would have to be kept somewhere else. No guide.
Not suitable: a sandbox session ends after one hour on the free plan and 24 hours on Pro, and n8n has to outlive its schedule.
Not documented. Modal is built for functions and short sandboxes, which end after at most 24 hours.
Not suitable: Vercel sandboxes are made for one task at a time, with no way to keep a web app running.
Run n8n and its database in Docker on one Droplet, keeping the encryption key yourself. A 2 vCPU / 4 GiB box at $24/month is the practical floor once the database is on the same machine.

picks.for: If you do not want a terminal
picks.why: The most complete one-click setup: n8n plus a managed PostgreSQL database and a public HTTPS address, inside the $19 monthly plan that comes back as usage.
picks.watch: The template does not set an encryption key; note the one n8n creates and keep it safe. It runs on Lizard's app platform, not at the sandbox sizes the calculator prices.

picks.for: If you want the cheapest one click
picks.why: The agent37-n8n template sets up n8n on its default 2 vCPU / 4 GB instance at $4.76 a month, with auto-sleep off by default.
picks.watch: It uses SQLite on the instance's disk rather than a separate database. Turning auto-sleep on stops scheduled workflows.

picks.for: If you can follow terminal steps
picks.why: CPU is billed only while it works, so an n8n that mostly waits is about $25 a month at 2 vCPU / 4 GiB, in a persistent sandbox with your own domain.
picks.watch: No n8n guide, one US region, and storage keeps billing while the machine is stopped.

usecases.outside: n8n's own [n8n Cloud](https://n8n.io/pricing/) costs €20 a month on Starter (2,500 workflow runs) and €50 on Pro (10,000), billed annually, with nothing to host. [Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing), a similar open-source tool, has a free plan and a $20 flat monthly plan. [Windmill](https://www.windmill.dev/docs/advanced/self_host) is free to host yourself and needs PostgreSQL.

usecases.title: Host your own Discord or Slack bot
usecases.seoTitle: Discord and Slack bot hosting: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I wrote a bot that answers questions in our Discord or Slack using an AI model, and I need somewhere for it to live.
usecases.standfirst: A chat bot is a small program that waits for messages, asks a model and replies. How Discord or Slack delivers those messages decides whether it can ever sleep. No provider hosts your own bot in one click; one provider's guide stands out, and the task-only sandboxes are a poor fit.
whatItIs: A support or community bot holds a login token for the chat app, receives each message, assembles some context, calls a model and posts the answer. You write it with a library such as [discord.js](https://github.com/discordjs/discord.js) or Slack's Bolt; the model runs elsewhere and is billed by its own provider.

Discord bots normally keep a **WebSocket** open to Discord: a connection that stays open so messages can be pushed down it at any moment. Discord calls these [persistent connections](https://discord.com/developers/docs/topics/gateway) that the bot must keep alive with regular heartbeats. Slack offers the same in [Socket Mode](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-socket-mode).

The other way is a public web address that Discord or Slack calls for each message ([Slack Request URLs](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-http-request-urls), [Discord interactions](https://discord.com/developers/docs/interactions/overview)). A bot built that way only needs to be awake when a message arrives. A bot that reads every message in a server needs the open connection, and so a machine that stays on.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Neither Discord nor Slack publishes one. 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 10 GiB runs Node or Python, a small history database and one model call at a time, with room for logs. Battleships models this job at 2 vCPU / 4 GiB / 20 GiB.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: Yes for a bot with an open connection: if it misses a heartbeat, Discord closes the connection, and a bot may only log in to it 1,000 times a day, so a host that keeps sleeping and waking it is a bad host. A bot that only answers through a web address can sleep if the host wakes it on a request.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The bot token (anyone with it controls the bot), conversation history and any settings. Lizard's guide keeps them in a database rather than the machine's disk, and warns to run only one copy per token, or every copy answers every message.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: No browser. Docker is optional. A database is recommended for history; SQLite (a single-file database) is enough for one copy. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Idle almost all the time, busy in short bursts when a message arrives. Battleships' always-on assistant averages about 6% CPU; one community server sees less traffic, so the calculator uses 3%.

routes.what: Not your own code: pick OpenClaw or Hermes on a Personal plan and connect it to your own Discord or Slack account, on Basic and above. The bot is that ready-made agent.
routes.price: Personal plans from $3.99 a month; Discord and Slack from the Basic plan

routes.what: The most complete official walkthrough: a discord.js example deployed with no public port, one copy per token, secrets, and a managed PostgreSQL database for history. Deployed from the command line.
An official example, but only for a bot that answers slash commands through a web address. Modal is not built to hold an open connection.
Boat documents the pattern: run the bot as a service that comes back by itself after a stop, resume or copy, and keep its public address. No bot-specific guide.
Turn off auto-hibernate, and turn off bot protection for that machine: it is on by default and "chat apps can't pass" it.
Create a sandbox with auto-stop off (the default is 15 idle minutes), install the bot and keep it running under a process manager. No bot guide.
A general Linux machine with Docker. Turn auto-pause off so the connection stays open. No bot guide.
A persistent sandbox never idle-pauses and can run the bot. No bot guide.
Turn idle pause off, or create the keep-awake file Sandboxer documents for work it cannot see, and run the bot as a service. No bot guide.
Only for a bot that answers through a web address: a Devbox wakes on a request, but an idle one is paused, which drops an open connection.
Only for a bot that answers through a web address: "services don't keep a Sprite from pausing", so a quiet connection would be paused.
A poor fit for an open connection: Blaxel treats a WebSocket with no traffic for 15 minutes as idle and puts the sandbox on standby. No bot guide.
A Worker can serve a Slack app that answers through a web address, but a Discord bot with an open connection does not fit a sandbox built around requests and stopping. No bot guide.
Not suitable: sessions end after one hour on the free plan and 24 hours on Pro.
Not suitable: sandboxes are made for one task and functions for one request, with no documented way to hold a connection open.
An always-on Droplet keeps the Discord or Slack gateway connected, because nothing idles or stops it. 1 vCPU / 2 GiB at $12/month is enough for one server.

picks.for: If you wrote the bot yourself
picks.why: The only provider with a full official Discord bot guide, including the database for history and the one-copy rule. It fits inside the $19 monthly plan that comes back as usage.
picks.watch: Deployed from the command line, and it runs on Lizard's app platform rather than the sandbox sizes the calculator prices.

picks.for: If you want to pay least for waiting
picks.why: CPU is billed only while it works, so a bot that mostly waits is about $12 a month at 1 vCPU / 2 GiB, in a sandbox that never idle-pauses.
picks.watch: No bot guide, one US region, and storage keeps billing while the machine is stopped.

picks.for: If you do not want to write code
picks.why: A ready-made AI agent (OpenClaw or Hermes) answering in your Discord or Slack, set up from the browser, from $3.99 a month with your own model key.
picks.watch: It is not your own bot: you configure an existing agent rather than run your code. These Personal plans are separate from the Cloud machines the calculator prices.

usecases.outside: An ordinary host such as [Render](https://render.com/pricing) runs an always-on background worker from $7 a month for 512 MB, or $25 for 1 CPU / 2 GB. A Slack app that answers through a web address fits [Cloudflare Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/): free up to 100,000 requests a day, or a $5 monthly minimum.

usecases.title: Give a small team Claude Code in the cloud
usecases.seoTitle: Claude Code in the cloud for a team: setup and costs
usecases.question: Three to five of us want Claude Code running on cloud machines, each with our own login, without sharing one account.
usecases.standfirst: Claude Code is built for one person on one machine. For a team that means one machine per developer, each signed in with that developer's own account. Five providers ship it preinstalled and one sets it up in one click; the catch is how logins are kept.
whatItIs: [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview) is Anthropic's coding agent. A developer starts it in a repository and asks for a change; it reads and edits files and runs commands and tests on the machine where it runs.

Vercel's guide puts the hosting constraint plainly: Claude Code "isn't built to be safe for multiple tenants: it's a command-line tool for one user, it keeps its state on disk" ([Vercel](https://vercel.com/docs/agent-harnesses/claude-code)). A shared machine would hold one person's login and mix everyone's unfinished work, so the default is one machine each.

For a team, three things have to be decided together: where each copy runs, whose Claude account pays, and what survives when a machine is replaced. The machine does not need to stay on; it runs while people work.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: Anthropic asks for 4 GB of memory or more and gives no CPU or disk minimum. Its own cloud sessions allow 4 vCPU, 16 GB and 30 GB of disk. 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 40 GiB per developer covers the agent, tests and a few containers, with room for their images.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No. Each machine runs during working hours: eight hours on 20 days is 160 hours each, or 800 for five developers. It can stop between sessions if its disk survives.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The repository and any work not yet pushed, and the login: on Linux, ~/.claude/.credentials.json. If the disk is thrown away, the developer signs in again and unpushed work is lost.

needs.label: Whose login
needs.value: On Claude's Team plan, "team members install Claude Code and log in with their claude.ai accounts", so each machine holds its owner's login. Some platforms store one Claude login for the whole account, which every sandbox uses: convenient alone, wrong for a team that wants usage and access per person.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Mostly waiting on the model: about 3% CPU on average in Battleships' software-factory workload, with peaks near half the machine during builds and tests.

routes.what: The agent37-claude-code template sets up one Claude Code instance on the developer's own Anthropic account. One instance each, so five developers means five; team management and roles are on the Max plan.
routes.price: Personal Pro $29.99 a month per instance; Max with team roles $99.99

routes.what: Claude Code is one of seven coding agents on every sandbox. Create one per developer from the dashboard or command line, then run claude.
Every machine ships with Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, and the console opens a terminal or desktop. No shared login feature, so each developer signs in on their own machine.
The default image includes Claude Code, Codex, Docker and a desktop. Open the machine's terminal from the dashboard. No Claude Code guide.
Claude Code is in the preinstalled agent list, Sandboxer publishes a Claude Code guide, and the dashboard has a Terminal tab.
A claude template and a guide. But "credentials belong to your Lizard account, not to a project, and every sandbox you start can use them": five machines would still share one Claude login.
An official command-line guide. The dashboard Playground opens a terminal in the browser, so nothing is installed locally, but setup is typed commands.
A prebuilt claude template and a guide, made for a fresh sandbox per task started from code rather than each developer's own machine.
An official guide that gives each Claude Code session its own sandbox, built in code.
An official guide: a Worker starts a sandbox where Claude Code edits a GitHub repository and returns the changes. Needs Workers and a container deployment.
A written tutorial for running Claude Code in a Blaxel sandbox against a codebase, with command-line and code steps.
An official example installs Claude Code in a Devbox with Anthropic's installer. Nothing on teams or logins.
A sandbox opens with a shell in the browser and can run it, but there is no Claude Code guide or template.
Sprites documents Claude Managed Agents, a different Anthropic product, not Claude Code. Installing it in a Sprite is by hand.
Not documented, and Modal sandboxes have no stopped state that keeps a developer's files.

One Droplet per developer, each with its own login and credentials; there is no shared team login. A powered-off Droplet is still billed, so five 4 vCPU / 8 GiB machines used eight hours a day cost the full month each unless you destroy them after work and restore from a snapshot.

picks.for: One machine per developer
picks.why: Claude Code preinstalled on a full virtual machine with Docker. Five 4 vCPU / 8 GB machines for 160 hours each come to about $29 of usage: the $20 plan plus about $9 from the wallet.
picks.watch: A stopped machine's disk is kept for only 14 days, so push work before a holiday. There is no free plan.

picks.for: If you want a guide and a dashboard terminal
picks.why: Claude Code preinstalled, an official guide, and a Terminal tab in the dashboard. The same five machines come to $40 a month.
picks.watch: Usage over the $20 plan is bought in $20 packs, and storage counts against an included quota: going over blocks new sandboxes.

picks.for: If the team does not want a terminal
picks.why: One-click Claude Code on each developer's own Anthropic account, so logins stay separate.
picks.watch: One instance per developer: five Pro instances are about $150 a month, and team roles need the $99.99 Max plan. These plans are separate from the Cloud machines the calculator prices.

usecases.outside: Anthropic runs Claude Code [cloud sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandbox-environments) on its own machines for Claude subscribers, with no separate machine price. [Claude Team](https://claude.com/pricing) is $25 per seat a month ($20 billed annually) for 2 to 150 people, with central billing, single sign-on and each member on their own login. Claude Enterprise starts at 20 seats, which is why a team of five starts on Team.

usecases.title: Run a scraper on a schedule
usecases.seoTitle: Run a scraper on a schedule: the cheapest cloud options
usecases.question: I want a script that checks a few websites four times a day and saves what it finds, without paying for a machine that sits idle.
usecases.standfirst: A scheduled scraper runs for minutes a day and is idle the rest. What matters is where the schedule lives and where the results go, not the machine. A schedule inside a sleeping machine does not fire, so look for providers whose platform starts the run.
whatItIs: A scraper fetches a set of pages, picks out the fields you care about (prices, listings, headlines) and writes them to a file or database. Pages that build themselves with JavaScript need a **headless browser**, a real browser such as Chromium running without a screen, driven by a tool like [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/intro). Plain pages only need a download.

The schedule is usually written as a **cron** expression, a short line such as "run at 6, 12, 18 and 24 o'clock" named after the Unix tool that runs jobs on a timetable. The key question is who keeps that clock. Agent 37 says it directly: "a crontab inside the container only runs while the container is running" ([Agent 37](https://www.agent37.com/docs/agents-api/crons)).

So there are two designs: a scheduler run by the platform that starts a fresh machine for each run (cheap), or a machine that stays on all month with its own timer (simple, and billed around the clock).

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: No vendor publishes one. 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 10 GiB fits a headless browser and logs; Battleships models one browser visit at 1 vCPU / 2 GiB / 5 GiB. Plain downloads fit in 1 GiB.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: No, if the schedule lives outside the machine. Four ten-minute runs a day is about 20 machine-hours a month, not 730. A timer inside the machine only works if the machine stays on.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: The results, kept outside the run: Runtime's jobs, for example, start "a fresh sandbox" every time and tell you to put data on a volume. Also cookies if a site needs a login, and a marker of what was already saved so a rerun does not duplicate rows.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: A browser only for pages built with JavaScript; it is the largest memory cost. Docker is optional. A database is optional on the machine but needed somewhere. No GPU.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Busy while a run is open: about 40% CPU in Battleships' scraping workload, because a browser does real work. Idle for the rest of the day.

routes.what: Lizard's sandboxes have no scheduler, but its one-click n8n template gives you n8n's Schedule Trigger and a PostgreSQL database for the results. Build the scrape as a workflow.
The best fit among the sandboxes: a schedule in a script, and the platform "wakes a sleeping machine, on standby or hibernated, shortly before" it is due. A missed slot runs once on wake.
Scheduled jobs run a command in a fresh sandbox on a cron, keep its output and exit code, and show up on a Jobs page in your account. Results go to a volume or your own storage.
The schedule is a Workers feature, Cron Triggers: the scheduled Worker can start a sandbox for the scrape. Each run gets up to 15 minutes of CPU on the paid plan.
Vercel Cron Jobs call a function, which can start a sandbox. The free Hobby plan runs crons only once a day, which is too rare here; Pro allows once a minute.

Platform crons fire "whether the instance is awake or asleep", but they wake an agent and give it a prompt, and are not offered on the base or n8n templates. For a script, the n8n template with auto-sleep off is the other route.
A schedule attaches to a Modal function written in code; the function can do the scrape or start a sandbox.
Sandbox schedules run a command inside a sandbox on a cron, with a run history; up to 100 per sandbox. Set up from code or the API.
No scheduler. A timer inside a machine left on works, but the machine is billed all month; otherwise something outside has to start a sandbox per run.
No scheduler found. A scheduler of your own calls Daytona's API to create a sandbox for each run.
No scheduler found. E2B is driven from code, so the schedule lives in your app or another service.
No scheduler found. A machine wakes on an API call or a visit to its public address, so an outside scheduler can start each run.
No scheduler found. An outside scheduler can wake a Devbox with a web request, but its own clock stops while it is paused.
No scheduler found. Idle pause and auto-stop are adjustable, so an outside scheduler plus the API is the route.
No scheduler found. The Tasks API keeps a Sprite awake during a run, but something outside has to start it.
cron inside a Droplet that stays on. DigitalOcean has no scheduler that starts a machine, so the idle hours between runs are billed at the full rate.

picks.for: If you want the machine to wake for the schedule
picks.why: The platform keeps the schedule and wakes the machine shortly before each run, so it can sleep in between. Four ten-minute runs a day is about $1.50 a month.
picks.watch: The schedule is written as a script file, and the $30 of starting credit needs a card.

picks.for: If you want a fresh machine each run
picks.why: Scheduled jobs start a clean sandbox on a cron and keep each run's output on a Jobs page. CPU is billed only while it works: about $0.50 a month here.
picks.watch: Nothing on a job's own disk survives the run; save results to a volume or your own database. One US region.

picks.for: If you do not want to write code
picks.why: The one-click n8n template gives you a visual schedule, web and browser steps, and a database for the results, inside the $19 monthly plan.
picks.watch: n8n stays on all month to keep its schedule, so it costs more than the run itself. It runs on Lizard's app platform, not the sandbox the calculator prices.

usecases.outside: Many scrapes need no sandbox at all. [Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/) can fetch and parse pages for free up to 100,000 requests a day, or within the $5 monthly paid plan. [Vercel Cron Jobs](https://vercel.com/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing) are included on every plan but run only once a day on Hobby. [Modal](https://modal.com/docs/guide/cron) schedules have no plan fee. [n8n's Schedule Trigger](https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/core-nodes/n8n-nodes-base.scheduletrigger) is free self-hosted, or from €20 a month on n8n Cloud.

usecases.title: Host your own MCP server
usecases.seoTitle: Host a remote MCP server: where to run it and what it costs
usecases.question: I built tools for Claude as an MCP server, and I want it at a web address so Claude can use them without anything running on my laptop.
usecases.standfirst: A remote MCP server is a small web service that gives an AI client your tools. It needs a public HTTPS address that answers, and very little else. One provider deploys one in a click, a few publish guides, and several providers' own MCP servers are something else entirely.
whatItIs: The [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/transports) (MCP) is how AI apps such as Claude find and use outside tools: search your documents, file a ticket, query a database. An **MCP server** is the program that offers those tools.

A local server runs on your own computer, started by the app. A remote one runs at a web address and speaks "Streamable HTTP", so Claude or [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp) can connect from anywhere. Claude's guide says a remote server "runs on infrastructure you host and is reachable over the internet" ([Claude](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building)).

Watch the wording on provider sites. Daytona, Sprites, Runtime and E2B all document MCP servers, but theirs let an AI agent control their sandboxes, or run MCP tools privately for your own agent. They are not a way to host your server for Claude.

needs.label: Machine size
needs.value: No vendor publishes one. A server whose tools call other services is a small web process: 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 10 GiB covers it, logs and an optional session store. A server whose tools run code or a browser should be sized like that work.

needs.label: Does it stay on?
needs.value: It must answer whenever the client calls. A host that sleeps can work if it wakes on the incoming request: Lizard's guide sleeps after 10 quiet minutes, and the first call afterwards takes longer. Claude allows 240 seconds per tool call.

needs.label: What must survive a restart
needs.value: Usually nothing: Cloudflare's template builds a fresh server for each request. If you use OAuth (a standard sign-in so only allowed users can connect), the signing keys and registered clients must survive, or every client has to sign in again.

needs.label: Browser, Docker, GPU
needs.value: No browser unless a tool drives one. Docker is optional. A database only if a tool needs one, and it can live elsewhere. No GPU: the model runs on the client's side.

needs.label: How busy it is
needs.value: Idle between tool calls and busy for milliseconds during one. There is no benchmark for it; the calculator uses 2%, below Battleships' 6% for an always-on agent, because the server only passes calls on.

routes.what: A Deploy to Workers button creates a remote MCP server at a workers.dev address ending in /mcp. This is a Cloudflare Worker, not the Sandbox product.

link.title: Cloudflare: build a remote MCP server

routes.price: Workers Free plan; Workers Paid from $5 a month

routes.what: A complete guide: Streamable HTTP, a token check so only your clients get in, a health check, a public HTTPS address and sleep when idle. Deployed from the command line.

link.title: Lizard: host a remote MCP server

routes.what: One command creates a TypeScript or Python MCP server, deployed as a Blaxel Function with a global web address. Command line, not dashboard.
An official example deploys a stateless MCP server, written in Python, as a Modal app.
A detailed guide runs each MCP server in its own sandbox at a private address with its own token. Suited to clients you control, not to Claude's web connector.

link.title: Sandboxer: one MCP server per sandbox

routes.what: Run the server and make its port public; Boat gives the port a public address that stays the same after resume. No custom domains, and no MCP guide.
A machine plus a self-serve custom domain, with HTTPS set up for you, makes a clean MCP host. No MCP guide.
A public port works and wakes a paused machine, but published ports have no login: "anyone can reach the whole service". Put the access check in the server. No MCP guide.
Public HTTP services and wake on request make a Devbox a workable host. No MCP guide.
Runtime's catalogue MCP servers run at private addresses for your own agent. Hosting yours for Claude is a normal sandbox with a custom domain; no guide.
No MCP template. A custom image can run the server, and every port gets a public agent37.app address. No MCP guide.
Daytona's own MCP server lets an AI agent control Daytona sandboxes. Hosting your own server is a manual install with no guide.
E2B's MCP gateway runs MCP tools inside a sandbox for your agent, which is the opposite direction. Sessions also end after one or 24 hours.
Sprites publishes a remote MCP server for controlling Sprites. Hosting yours means a service on a port, which wakes on a request; no guide.
A sandbox port gets a public address, but sandboxes are made for one task and end; a Vercel Function would be the simpler host. No MCP guide.
A small Droplet with a public IPv4 answers at a stable address all month. DigitalOcean's own MCP server manages DigitalOcean resources; it does not host your server.

picks.for: If you do not want a terminal
picks.why: The only one-click route: a Deploy to Workers button creates a working remote MCP server, free up to 100,000 requests a day.
picks.watch: It is a Worker, not a sandbox, so the calculator's Cloudflare Sandbox price does not apply. The free plan allows 10 ms of CPU per request, enough for tools that call other services but not for heavy ones.

picks.for: If you want a guide that covers access
picks.why: The most complete guide, including a token check and sleep when idle, so a quiet server costs little. Inside the $19 monthly plan that comes back as usage.
picks.watch: Its sample token expires after an hour and the signing key is not saved; use your own token issuer for a lasting server.

picks.for: If you want an always-on machine and your own domain
picks.why: CPU is billed only while it works, so a small server answering all month is about $6, with a custom domain.
picks.watch: No MCP guide; you set up the server, HTTPS address and access check yourself. One US region.

picks.for: A small always-on MCP endpoint on a known address
picks.why: $6 a month buys a 1 vCPU / 1 GiB Droplet with a public IPv4, any TCP port except SMTP, and no idle stop to wake from.
picks.watch: There is no hard spend cap and no tokenised URL: you add TLS and authentication yourself, and a spend alert only emails you.

usecases.outside: [Cloudflare Workers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/) on their own are the cheapest home: free up to 100,000 requests a day, or a $5 monthly minimum. [Vercel Functions](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/pro-plan) are free on Hobby, with a $20 monthly Pro fee. [Render](https://render.com/pricing) runs an always-on web service from $7 a month for 512 MB.
